title: The Air Pocket
passages:
Dey had the name in his mouth and nothing behind it.

"Ivo Salas," he said, agreeable, the way a man hands over a tool he's been asked to hold. Behind his teeth Wren's voice came through the bone of his jaw, thin and flat, the way her voice always arrived down here, less a sound than a pressure: *Dey. Say something to her that's yours.*

"Where is he." Nia hadn't let go of the crank. She was maybe fourteen, in a man's coat cut down to her, and her right hand was locked around a wooden grip worn pale and smooth as a tooth. Bolted to the side of the white enamel chest was a spring cell — wind the crank, store the tension, let it unwind slow to keep the inside cold — and the gauge on it sat in the last quarter of its arc. "He said Tuesday. He said he'd bring a winch and a man with a boat and take us up. Where is he."

"He lent me air," Dey said.

He lifted the pony bottle on his chest rig, a stubby aluminum thing the size of a thermos with S.S. scratched into the shoulder, and turned it so her lamp caught the scratches. His exhaust ticked. That was the scrubber's relief valve letting go each time he breathed out — the rebreather stripped the carbon dioxide out of his air with a canister of sodalime and gave the rest back, so every breath he took down here was a breath somebody else had already used. The mouthpiece tasted of another man's spit. He'd been grateful for it for an hour and now he couldn't have said why.

"He gave me this at forty-two meters and told me to keep going down," Dey said. "So I did."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the whole answer I've got."

Nia's jaw worked. "He had a beard. Bad knee, he sat down on the stair to rest it. He put my brother in that box and swore on his mother he'd come back with a ride." She tipped her head at the chest without taking her eyes off Dey. Under the fogged glass of the inner lid a small boy lay in a nest of foil blankets with a mask over his face, and the fog bloomed and thinned, bloomed and thinned. "So don't stand in my ward breathing his air and tell me his name like it's a coin you found."

*Rude,* Wren said in his jaw. *And correct. Dey, back off the chest, two meters, hands where she can see them.*

"Copy," Dey said, and took a step toward her.

He watched himself do it. That was the part he'd have told her if he'd had the words: he could see his own boot going forward on the tile, and he agreed with it, and the agreement had nothing to do with him. He was warm. That was wrong too. Fifty-two meters down, in a ward with a ceiling of standing water and a curtain rail furred with silt, he was warm as a kitchen, and calm, and it would have taken a better man than Dey Okafor to be frightened on purpose.

Nia saw it. He watched her see it — her eyes going to his, then to the lamp, then back, checking whether he was tracking, and not liking the answer. She'd seen the deep do this. He could tell by the way she stopped arguing and started measuring.

"Say my name," she said.

"You haven't given it."

"Say his."

Dey reached for the man and got a shape with the middle missing. A cough, wet at the bottom of it. A hand pushing a bottle across something. A voice saying *keep going down*, which was the only sentence that had survived, and it had come loose from whoever said it.

"Ivo Salas," he said, warm and helpful, holding out the borrowed bottle. "He's a friend of yours?"

Nia's hand stayed on the crank. Her other one went flat against the glass over her brother's mask, and she said, very quietly, "Oh, you're *gone*."

The tick stopped.

Not slowed — stopped. For an hour the scrubber's relief valve had been letting go in Dey's exhaust, a dry little *tick* every time he breathed out, keeping time in the hinge of Wren's jaw like a clock in the next room. Now the room was quiet. The tether stood stiff over the helipad rail, the wind came off the water in long cold shoves, and down the bone line there was nothing at all. No tick. No breath to make one.

"Dey." She had the slate open on her knee — the recorder that logged everything a diver saw and did — and its screen showed the flat green line of a man not breathing. Four years she'd worked from the other side of that line. A diver came up hollow, missing an hour, and she took his slate home and built the hour back for him, cleaned it up, spliced the parts that would gut him out at the seam so what he heard was true but survivable. She was good at it. She had never once done it live. "Dey, breathe in on my mark. In—"

Nothing.

"You are not doing this to me on a Tuesday," she said. "In. Now."

Down in the ward Nia's hand was flat against the glass and Dey was watching her, warm and agreeable, a man watching weather come in. Wren could see all of it through his own eyes on the feed — the fogged lid, the girl, the gauge in the last quarter of its arc — and she could not reach the part of him that had quit. There was no take to redo. No seam to splice. If he went, he went in the only version there was.

"In," she said, softer, the way you'd talk to something standing on a ledge. "And out. That's all it ever is. You've done it your whole life. In—"

The tick came back. One, small and dry, and the green line lifted and fell.

Wren put her forehead against the cold rail for exactly one second. Then she keyed the boat channel. "Sol. It's not cargo." Her voice came out level, which she'd be proud of later. "The twelve-thousand case is two kids. A girl, maybe fourteen. A boy in the box, small, on a mask. That's the manifest. That's the whole thing the Factor's paying for."

Sol didn't answer. Wren could feel her not answering, the whole boat holding still around it.

"Copy," Sol said finally. Just that.

That was when the drone came down through the hatch.

It dropped out of the standing water overhead without a splash too small to matter — a broker's thing the size of two fists, four rotors and a lens on a little gimbal — and hung in the air a meter above Dey's head. The lens turned down. A voice came out of it, pleasant, the Factor's own, thinned by water and distance: *"Manifest confirms. One sealed cryo unit. Seals intact. Count: one."* The lens ticked as it counted, patient, thorough. *"Value confirmed. Awaiting ascent."*

On the helipad Wren watched Sol watch the tether. The captain's face did nothing at all.

Her thumb came off the brake.
